headline: Rental market remains tight with rents up ~6% over 12 months; landlords reassessing cash flow positions as falling prices erode asset values but rental yields stay elevated
reasoning: While falling property prices are improving purchase affordability at the margin, they are not translating into rental relief — rents have risen approximately 6% over the last 12 months and vacancy rates remain historically tight. Landlords are reassessing their cash flow positions and adjusting rents upward. This dynamic is creating hardship for renters even as buyers hesitate. The dislocation between purchase price declines and rising rents is a key tension in the market.
quote: Obviously falling prices helps affordability. The flip side of that is it's not helping affordability in terms of rentals. We're really seeing some challenges for renters and rents have gone up about 6% the last 12 months and a lot of landlords are reassessing their cash flow positions and the rents as well.
episode_title: What will attract investors back to the property market?

headline: Investors recalibrating toward higher-yield established properties or new builds with negative gearing and tax benefits; also considering other asset classes as property loses its appeal
reasoning: Property investors who have stepped back from the market are now re-evaluating what they would need to re-enter. They are targeting established properties with significantly higher rental yields or new builds where negative gearing and tax depreciation benefits apply. New property purchases by investors are adding competition in segments traditionally dominated by first home buyers. Notably, some investors are also looking at alternative asset classes entirely, suggesting structural reallocation away from residential property.
quote: Investors are absolutely recalibrating the type of properties they're looking for. They're looking for properties with either a much higher rental yield if it's an established property, or they're looking for purchasing a new property where they will get the negative gearing benefits and the tax benefits. So investors are sitting on the sidelines looking for the higher rental properties as well as some of the new properties. Those new properties are traditionally areas that first home buyers are in. So it's adding a little bit of competition there. I think to be frank, investors are looking at other asset classes as well.
episode_title: What will attract investors back to the property market?

headline: All buyer segments — investors, first home buyers, downsizers — have ground to a halt; no spring rebound expected; every major capital city except Darwin fell 3.1% nationally in the last quarter
reasoning: Investors have essentially stopped participating in the market, first home buyers are paralysed by affordability pressures and fears of negative equity (many borrowing up to 95% LVR), and older downsizers are holding onto properties rather than listing. Listings are down about 15% on the prior year even heading into the traditionally busy spring season. Every major capital city except Darwin recorded falls in values last quarter, with a national decline of 3.1%. Anthony does not expect a meaningful rebound in spring.
quote: In terms of credit flows, investors literally have stopped. Investors are totally out of the market in broader terms... First home buyers is interesting because a big part of what the government talked about was trying to help first home buyers into the market. But first home buyers are looking to see what they can do. They still have genuine affordability pressures. They're still genuinely concerned about interest rate rises and they're actually very concerned about a falling market. Some first home buyers go up to 95% loan to value ratio. There's a lot of concern with first time buyers around negative equity. So all segments of the market right now have really ground to a halt. And to be honest, I don't think we're going to see much of a rebound this spring.
episode_title: What will attract investors back to the property market?

headline: Australian residential housing market in broad-based decline: $34B wiped in June quarter, 93% of capital city suburbs falling in winter versus 45% in autumn, clearance rates down from 70%+ to ~50% at spring open
reasoning: ABS data shows $34 billion was wiped off the residential housing market in the June quarter. In autumn, 45% of capital city suburbs declined in value; by winter that figure rose to 93%, indicating a much more widespread decline. Spring clearance rates nationally were around 50%, compared to over 70% the prior year. Macro headwinds including low GDP, stubborn inflation, tax changes, and the prospect of another rate rise have brought the market to a near standstill. Some commentators are forecasting a 10–15% peak-to-trough drop.
quote: Some of the data started to flow through since obviously the budget and other factors, the June quarter, the ABS data shows that $34 billion has been wiped off the residential housing market for the quarter. So that's a significant drop in values. If we dive into that a little bit more, in autumn we saw 45% of capital city suburbs decline in value. In winter that was up to 93%. So what we're seeing is a much more widespread decline. We obviously had the start of spring that's normally one of the busiest times of year clearance rates this time comparatively last year were over 70%. First weekend of spring nationally there were about 50%. So the market on the back of the tax changes, low GDP, stubborn inflation and talk of another rate rise... has really brought the market to a standstill. In fact, some commentators are now talking about a 10 to 15% peak to through drop.
episode_title: What will attract investors back to the property market?

headline: Australian house prices forecast to fall 5-10% peak to trough as tax changes on capital gains and negative gearing freeze investor activity
reasoning: Landahl explains that changes to capital gains tax and negative gearing have effectively stopped investors in their tracks, though investors with existing property are not selling, reducing liquidity. Investors still active are pivoting toward higher-yielding properties given the changed after-tax return profile. Sydney and Melbourne are recording negative growth, while Perth and Brisbane are also falling, with most market forecasters pencilling in a 5-10% annualised peak-to-trough decline. He warns of significant unintended consequences including rising rents, low vacancy rates, and a looming supply crisis for renters as new investor-funded stock fails to come to market.
quote: Perth Brisbane and our falling Sydney and Melbourne are recording are negative growth at the moment. So most are forecasting 5 to 10% annualized from peak to trough. Ah fall in growth. Is that bringing home buyers back in the market? I think it's creating opportunities for home buyers because the market has slowed. But I think there's a lot of unintended consequences around it's investors are holding stock are there's not new investment stock coming. So there's a massive issue looming for renters. We're already seeing low vacancy rates. We're already seeing rents rising. Investors in the market are looking for higher yielding properties now because their strategy has changed. So I don't think the full consequence of the tax changes have played out yet. But the market has. The market is falling, and I think we're going to see a few more months of pretty slow activity in the market.
episode_title: The implications of falling mortgage applications

He also observes self-managed super funds being used by business owners to acquire commercial property as an investment. Despite this credit strength, many businesses have been absorbing rising input costs rather than passing them through to consumers, which he flags as a potential source of lagged inflationary pressure downstream.

Um, a lot of businesses have been looking at working capital facilities, but we are seeing seeing businesses now looking at term loans, growth strategies, buying premises. We're also looking at business owners with self-managed super funds, looking at premises as well as an investment option. So commercial credit is quite strong. A lot of business owners haven't passed through to the consumer yet, some of the costs. So businesses have been absorbing a lot of the costs are increases that have come into their business. So they could be a lag there on some inflationary forces as well.

headline: Landahl expects one more RBA rate rise, likely around November, driven by sticky inflation, elevated government spending and rising construction costs
reasoning: Landahl notes that RBA Governor Michele Bullock was less hawkish on rate rises but remained very concerned about inflation and recalibrated forward forecasts in a way that leaves another hike on the table. He points to government spending running at 3.1% above the RBA's target range, geopolitical pressure on fuel prices, and rising construction costs as factors that make another rate rise probable. His personal instinct is that the RBA probably needs another rate rise despite the pain for mortgage holders, and he nominates November as the likely timing.
quote: I think she made no doubt that if some of those forward forecasts were hit that they would see another rate rise. The markets variously affected in probably one more rate rise. Now that may be down the track. There might be a lag effect a little bit with fuel prices. Construction costs are on the rise. My instinct is there'll be another rate rise. To be honest with you. And they probably need another rate rise. As much as we don't want one for a mortgage holder. Ah, just with inflation, government spending at 3.1%, which is actually above the RBA's target range. So we got out. We got government spending out of control. We got fuel prices being impacted by geopolitical events overseas. We've got construction costs rising. So yes, house prices are falling. Rents are going up. So it's a challenging environment. And I think we might see another rate rise maybe around November.
